Shell Asset Atlas: explainer storyboard

5:35, 11 chapters, 36 narrated lines. Every frame here is the real application, captured by film/render.py while it pressed the real controls, and the narration and timing come from film/scenes.py. Numbers come from the data built 2026-11-11.

Unofficial portfolio project. Not affiliated with, or endorsed by, Shell plc. The narration uses a synthetic voice.

0:00Under one platform

Shows
A cold open on the app's subsea view: the descent from the sea surface at Perdido, down the water column and in among the well paths. Then the title
Camera
No cursor. The app's own dive camera, opened from its deep link and slowed to three-quarter speed. The title fades up, the picture fades to black behind it, and the film cuts to a fresh load of the app: the globe arriving from space.
Sound
The pad fades in under the first line.

0:00This is the water under one platform in the US Gulf. 2,388 metres of it.

0:07And below the seabed: 80 wellbores, almost all of them drawn from survey records that anyone can download.

0:15This is the Shell Asset Atlas. An unofficial project, with no connection to Shell, built entirely from public data.

0:24Public records, one globe

Shows
The turning globe and the headline figures in the side panel: production, installations, pipelines
Camera
The cursor appears and passes down the figures as each is named. The globe keeps turning.
Sound
Pad only.

0:24Operators report what they produce to public regulators, every month. The atlas puts those records on a globe.

0:31210 installations and sites. 48 oil and gas fields. About 5,900 kilometres of pipeline. Drawn from regulators in the United States, the United Kingdom and Norway.

0:45Every column is a hub

Shows
Fly to the US Gulf, point at a production tower for its sparkline, click it for the full record
Camera
The cursor presses the US Gulf chip and the app flies in and tilts. It glides to the Mars tower, the hover card appears, and a click opens the details drawer.
Sound
A tick on each click.

0:45Start in the US Gulf. Each column is a production hub, and its height is what that hub produced in a month.

0:52Click one for its record. This is Mars: a tension-leg platform, standing in 894 metres of water since 1996, with every month of production since 2015.

1:06A decade you can replay

Shows
The production timeline plays from the first month to the latest. The towers, the leaderboard and the storm tracks follow it
Camera
The drawer is closed to reveal the leaderboard. The cursor presses play and waits on the button while the decade runs, then moves to the total.
Sound
A tick on play.

1:07Now press play. A decade of production replays, month by month, and the leaderboard re-ranks as it goes.

1:14By December 2025, the total is about a million barrels of oil equivalent a day, gross. But look at the dips on the way. Several of them are storms.

1:27What a hurricane does

Shows
The Gulf storms panel and the replay of Hurricane Ida: its track drawn across the Gulf, the towers falling in the month after, and the estimate of what was deferred
Camera
The cursor scrolls the side panel to the storm list and clicks Ida. The app jumps to the month before, flies to the Gulf and plays the storm through; the film shows that replay at two-fifths speed. The cursor then reads the hub-by-hub estimate and the weekly forecast snapshot.
Sound
Ticks on clicks.

1:28The atlas follows 26 Gulf storms that passed near Shell structures. The costliest was Hurricane Ida.

1:35Click it, and the atlas goes back to July 2021. Ida crosses the Gulf in August as a category four hurricane, and its centre passes two kilometres from the nearest Shell structure.

1:47The month after, Shell-operated production in the Gulf falls by more than half. Mars goes from about 182 thousand barrels of oil equivalent a day to nothing, and takes three months to recover.

2:01Across two hubs, the atlas estimates about 10 million barrels of oil equivalent deferred, relative to the pre-storm baseline. It's an estimate, and the panel says so.

2:12Each week, it also checks the National Hurricane Center's feed. At the last check, no storm was active.

2:19Against every other operator

Shows
The peer benchmark: every operator in the US Gulf ranked by operated production, re-ranking as the decade plays, then the same for Norway
Camera
The B key opens the benchmark. The cursor scrubs the timeline back to its first month and presses play, pauses on the month after Ida, plays on to the latest month, then switches the basin to Norway and reads the note.
Sound
Ticks on clicks and a soft tick on the key.

2:19The regulator publishes every operator, not only Shell. Press B, and the atlas ranks them all.

2:25Go back to 2015 and play the decade again. This time the bars are companies, ranked by the production they operate.

2:39Stop at September 2021, the month after Ida. BP has taken the lead.

2:45By December 2025, Shell ranks number one of 30 operators in the US Gulf, with about 28 percent of operated production. It has led in 123 of these 132 months.

3:00It isn't first everywhere. In Norway, Shell ranks number five, far behind Equinor. And this is production by operator of record, not equity.

3:09Below the waterline

Shows
Search for Perdido, press Dive below, and the subsea view: the water column to scale, the surveyed well paths, the depth staff, the depth stretch, colour by spud year, a turn of the camera and a well's own record
Camera
The cursor switches to the seabed map, searches for Perdido and presses Dive below. It is hidden for the descent, which the film shows at three-fifths speed. The view then orbits by itself while the cursor reads the figures, presses Depth x3 and Spud year, drags the scene round and points at one well.
Sound
Ticks on clicks, soft ticks on keys. Nothing is added for the descent.

3:10Now, the place this film began. Search for Perdido: a spar, moored in 2,388 metres of water.

3:18Its record has one more button. Dive below.

3:21Everything here is drawn to true scale. The water is as deep as 2.9 Burj Khalifas, stood on end.

3:28Then the seabed, and below it, 80 wellbores. 76 of them follow the directional surveys filed with the regulator. The rest are drawn dashed, as schematics.

3:39The deepest ends 6,337 metres below sea level. Together, they come to about 157 kilometres of drilled hole.

3:50Stretch the depth three times, and each path is easier to follow.

3:56Colour them by the year drilling began, and the field grows in front of you, from 2002 to 2025.

4:03Drag to look around. Then point at any well for its name, its depth and its status.

4:11The atlas draws only what is public. The seabed is interpolated from well-site depths, and no geology is shown, because none is published.

4:21Gross is not net

Shows
Back on the globe: the leaderboard as a way in, a partner-held field, Shell's equity in it and its net share
Camera
Escape closes the record. The cursor presses Troll at the top of the leaderboard and the app flies to Norway. The cursor passes over the gross and net figures, then along the chart's net line.
Sound
Ticks on clicks.

4:22Back on the surface, Troll, off Norway, tops the leaderboard. But Shell doesn't operate it. It holds about 8 percent.

4:29So the atlas shows Shell's net figure beside the gross one. Gross is never passed off as net.

4:35Beyond the wellhead

Shows
The night-lights basemap, the hand-placed sites around Rotterdam, the fuel station heatmap and the 3D retail skyline
Camera
Escape closes the record. The cursor switches to Night, presses the Europe chip and 3D retail, and the app tilts into the skyline. Orbit starts the camera turning.
Sound
Ticks on clicks.

4:36Beyond production, 26 more sites are placed by hand, from LNG plants and refineries to hydrogen and wind.

4:44And on the street, OpenStreetMap volunteers have mapped more than 28 thousand Shell-branded fuel stations. One click turns them into a skyline.

4:55Nothing taken on trust

Shows
Data & method: every source with its licence and fetch status, and the method notes
Camera
The cursor presses Data & method, reads down the source table, scrolls through the method notes and closes the dialog.
Sound
Ticks on clicks.

4:55None of it has to be taken on trust. Data and method lists every source, with its licence.

5:01A pipeline rebuilds the atlas from them every week. If a regulator's site is down, it falls back to the last good copy, and says so.

5:14One globe

Shows
Back out to the whole world, then the end card with sources and the disclaimer
Camera
The cursor puts the map back as it found it, presses the World chip and leaves. The app flies back out to the globe and the end card fades up.
Sound
The pad fades out under the last line.

5:14The Shell Asset Atlas. Public records, on one globe, from the sea surface to the bottom of the deepest well.

5:22It's an unofficial project, and it isn't endorsed by Shell. The data belongs to the regulators, and to OpenStreetMap's contributors. This narration is a synthetic voice.
